questions.stem: How does Ghost Wall begin?
options: With a short prologue in which a young Iron Age woman is led out to be sacrificed
With Silvie arriving at university in Manchester to begin studying archaeology
With Bill teaching a class of local schoolchildren about the Roman invasion of Britain
With police officers searching a bog in Northumberland for a missing student
questions.explanation: The prologue imagines an ancient sacrifice in a bog. It casts a shadow over the whole novel, and the ending echoes it.

questions.stem: Why are Silvie and her parents in Northumberland?
options: They have moved there so that Bill can work as a guide at Hadrian's Wall
They are visiting relatives who farm land next to an archaeological dig
They join a university course that is re-enacting Iron Age life for two weeks
They are on a family walking holiday that Bill has planned along Hadrian's Wall
questions.explanation: Silvie, Bill and Alison join Professor Slade and three students in an experiment in living as Iron Age Britons did. For Bill, it is a chance to live out his obsession.

questions.stem: What does daily life at the camp involve?
options: Living in a roundhouse, wearing rough tunics, foraging and cooking over a fire
Living in modern tents, digging for artefacts and cataloguing them each night
Living in a farmhouse, reading Iron Age texts and writing essays about them
Living in a roundhouse, but cooking and eating with modern supplies from the village
questions.explanation: The group forages, hunts and cooks with Iron Age methods. The women do most of the cooking and gathering, while the men hunt, a division Silvie notices.

questions.stem: Why does Bill beat Silvie partway through the novel?
options: He discovers she has hidden a radio in the roundhouse to listen to music
He learns that she has told Professor Slade she wants to leave the camp
He catches her bathing in the stream, which he says is shameful
He finds out she has been phoning her school friends from the village
questions.explanation: Bill punishes Silvie with his belt after he finds her bathing. The violence is told from inside Silvie's mind, which matches Moss's aim of never showing abuse from the abuser's view.

questions.stem: What do Silvie and Molly do that breaks the rules of the re-enactment?
options: They telephone Silvie's grandmother and ask her to come and take them home
They walk to a modern shop in the village, where they meet a local woman, Trudi
They take Professor Slade's car and drive out to the coast for a whole day by the sea
They hide modern clothes in the roundhouse and secretly wear them after dark
questions.explanation: The trip gives Silvie a taste of freedom and of Molly's easy confidence. Trudi, a midwife, later becomes part of Silvie's rescue.

questions.stem: What is the 'ghost wall' that the group builds?
options: A ring of standing stones raised to honour the gods believed to live in the bog
A palisade of bare wooden stakes built to keep wild animals out of the camp
A palisade topped with skulls, copying an ancient defence against the Romans
A stone wall built along the line of Hadrian's Wall to mark the old frontier
questions.explanation: Ancient Britons were said to have set up palings topped with ancestors' skulls as a magical defence. The group builds one with animal skulls, and the night of drumming around it marks a turn toward something darker.

questions.stem: What do Bill and the professor decide to re-enact near the end of the novel?
options: An Iron Age wedding, with Silvie as the young bride
A Roman attack on the camp, with the students as soldiers
An Iron Age burial, with a skeleton taken from a museum
An Iron Age human sacrifice, with Silvie as the victim
questions.explanation: The men's interest in bog sacrifice turns into a plan to act one out. Silvie is chosen, which brings the prologue's violence into the present.

questions.stem: How is Silvie rescued?
options: Silvie unties herself and runs to a farm across the moor
Her mother stops the ritual and leads her away from the bog
Dan persuades the professor to let her go before it is too late
Molly gets help, and Trudi and the police arrive in time
questions.explanation: Molly, horrified by the plan, slips away and brings help. The rescue comes from outside the group, which shows how far the people inside it had gone along.

questions.stem: How does the novel end?
options: Silvie stays at the camp alone to finish the re-enactment
Silvie spends the night at Trudi's cottage, with Molly beside her
Silvie returns home with her parents as if nothing had happened
Silvie leaves for university in London and never sees her father again
questions.explanation: The ending is quiet and open. Silvie is safe for now, but readers are left to wonder what her future holds.

questions.stem: How does the novel's structure link the past and the present?
options: The prologue is set after the main story, revealing what becomes of Silvie
The prologue's ancient sacrifice is mirrored by the near-sacrifice of Silvie at the end
Each chapter alternates between an Iron Age family's life and Silvie's family in the present
The novel moves backwards in time, ending with the arrival of the Romans in Britain
questions.explanation: The ending repeats the opening in a modern setting. The mirroring suggests that the violence of the past has not gone away.

questions.stem: Who narrates Ghost Wall?
options: Professor Slade, in his field notes
Silvie, the seventeen-year-old daughter
Molly, one of the university students
Bill, Silvie's father, in a diary
questions.explanation: Silvie tells the story in the first person. We see her father's control from inside the fear it creates.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Bill Hampton?
options: A self-taught historian who is strict with his family but not violent toward any of them
A farmer who resents the students for camping on his land without asking
A retired soldier who teaches survival skills to young people every summer
A bus driver obsessed with ancient Britain, who controls his family through violence
questions.explanation: Bill is self-taught and passionate about the Iron Age, but he uses it to justify control, racism and violence. Moss has said she did not want him to be simply a monster, but shaped by the world around him.

questions.stem: How is Silvie's mother, Alison, presented?
options: As fiercely protective, standing up to Bill whenever he threatens Silvie
As an expert on the Iron Age, who leads the women's foraging trips
As quietly rebellious, secretly helping Silvie plan her escape
As fearful and submissive, accepting Bill's control and even excusing it
questions.explanation: Alison has learned to survive Bill by obeying him. She tends to blame Silvie for provoking him, which shows how abuse can turn its victims against each other.

questions.stem: What role does Molly play in Silvie's story?
options: A confident student who sees Bill clearly and helps Silvie imagine a freer life
A confident student who is charmed by Bill and comes to adopt his views
A student who sides with Bill and reports Silvie's rule-breaking to him
A student who stays aloof from Silvie throughout, treating her as a child to be ignored
questions.explanation: Molly calls Bill's behaviour what it is and challenges him. Silvie is drawn to her, and in the end Molly is the one who brings help.

questions.stem: How is Professor Slade presented as the novel goes on?
options: As a voice of reason who holds Bill's violence in check right up until the very end
As an educated man whose learning leads him to question Bill's methods
As a careless academic who barely notices what is happening at the camp
As an educated man who is drawn into Bill's violence instead of stopping it
questions.explanation: Slade begins as the polite academic in charge, but he bonds with Bill and helps plan the sacrifice. Class and education, the novel suggests, do not protect anyone from cruelty.

questions.stem: What is the irony of Silvie's full name, Sulevia?
options: Bill chose it as a Roman name, but it turns out to be the name of a Celtic king
Bill chose it to honour his mother, but she was named after a Roman empress
Bill chose it as a modern name, but it turns out to be thousands of years old
Bill chose it as truly British, but Sulevia was a local goddess the Romans adopted
questions.explanation: Bill wants a pure, native name for his daughter, but Sulevia, a goddess of springs, was taken up by the Romans. The name itself undermines his idea of an unmixed British past.

questions.stem: When is Ghost Wall set?
options: In the 1960s
In the 2010s
In the 1990s
In the 1940s
questions.explanation: Moss set the novel in the 1990s in a poor part of northern England. Readers in 2018, the year of publication, often connected it to debates about Brexit.

questions.stem: Why do many readers connect Ghost Wall with Brexit?
options: Bill's belief in a pure native Britain echoes the nationalism of the Brexit debate
The novel is set during the referendum and follows its campaign closely
Moss wrote it as a direct allegory of the 2016 campaign and its leaders
Its rural setting celebrates the English countryside that many Leave voters valued highly
questions.explanation: The novel is set years earlier, but its fears about borders, outsiders and an imagined pure past spoke to readers in 2018. Moss has said it is about nationalism more broadly, not only Brexit.

questions.stem: What are 'bog bodies', which haunt the novel?
options: Ancient human remains, often of people killed in rituals, preserved in peat bogs
Fossils of extinct animals found in the deep mud along the Northumberland coast
Roman soldiers buried in mass graves beside Hadrian's Wall after a battle
Wooden statues of gods that Iron Age people sank in lakes as offerings
questions.explanation: The acid, airless peat preserves bodies for thousands of years, sometimes showing how they died. The prologue imagines one such killing.

questions.stem: How does class shape Silvie's situation?
options: Unlike the students, she cannot take university, travel or freedom for granted
Like the students, she has already travelled widely and plans to study overseas
Unlike the students, she comes from a wealthy family who own the land
Like the professor, she grew up surrounded by books and academic talk
questions.explanation: The students talk easily about universities and trips abroad. Silvie has never been overseas, and her father limits her chances, so the gap between them is sharp.

questions.stem: Which theme is most central to Ghost Wall?
options: The way men use history and tradition to justify control and violence
The value of preserving ancient skills that modern life has lost
The joy of returning to a simple life close to nature and the seasons
The danger of academic study that cuts people off from real life
questions.explanation: Bill uses an imagined Iron Age to excuse his control of his wife and daughter. The novel shows how stories about the past can serve power in the present.

questions.stem: What does the ghost wall suggest about walls and borders?
options: They protect communities, as the first ghost walls held back the Romans
They belong to the ancient past and have little meaning for people in the present day
They keep the modern world out, giving the camp a true taste of the past
They mark who belongs and who is an outsider more than they keep anyone safe
questions.explanation: The original ghost walls were a desperate, magical defence that did not stop the Romans. Moss links walls to the urge to divide insiders from outsiders, then and now.

questions.stem: How does the novel explore complicity?
options: Several people go along with Bill's violence, through fear, loyalty or excitement
Bill alone is responsible, since the others know nothing of his plans
The students resist Bill as a group, while Alison and the professor go along with him
Silvie herself willingly helps the men plan her own sacrifice
questions.explanation: Alison obeys, the professor joins in, and some of the students go along with the ritual. Even Silvie feels the pull of the chanting, which shows how group violence draws people in.

questions.stem: How does Silvie change over the course of the novel?
options: She moves from open rebellion toward gradually accepting her father's view of the past
She moves from trusting Molly toward siding with her father against her
She moves from fearful obedience toward open, violent defiance of her father
She moves from fearful obedience toward seeing her father's control for what it is
questions.explanation: At first Silvie defends her father against Molly's criticism. Her growing friendship with Molly helps her see the abuse clearly, a coming-of-age story under pressure.

questions.stem: What is unusual about how Moss presents dialogue?
options: She reports speech indirectly, so no character's exact words appear
She gives Bill's speech quotation marks but leaves others' unmarked
She uses no quotation marks, so speech runs into Silvie's narration
She uses quotation marks for Silvie's speech but not for anyone else's
questions.explanation: Without speech marks, other voices, especially Bill's, flow straight into Silvie's thoughts. It shows how deeply his words have got inside her head.

questions.stem: What is the effect of Silvie's first-person narration?
options: Readers experience Bill's violence from inside the fear of the person he hurts
Readers see every event from a cool distance, as a scientist would record it
Readers learn what every character secretly thinks and feels at once
Readers share Silvie's view of the camp as an exciting adventure
questions.explanation: Silvie's voice is guarded and close. Moss keeps us inside the victim's mind, not watching from the outside, so we feel the threat as she does.

questions.stem: How does Moss build tension in such a short novel?
options: Through multiple narrators whose versions of events directly contradict each other
Through constant foreshadowing, from the prologue to the talk of sacrifice and skulls
Through a series of cliffhangers in which characters vanish at the end of chapters
Through long flashbacks that slowly reveal a crime committed years earlier
questions.explanation: The prologue, the bog, the skulls and the men's fascination with sacrifice all point toward the ending. Readers dread what is coming long before Silvie does.

questions.stem: How does Moss use the landscape of moor, river and bog?
options: As a peaceful pastoral idyll that contrasts with the cruelty of the human characters
As a safe refuge where Silvie can escape from her father's close control
As a symbol of modern Britain's progress away from its violent past
As a beautiful but threatening place where the past lies close to the surface
questions.explanation: The bog preserves the dead and keeps old violence close by. The isolation of the landscape also leaves Silvie with nowhere to run.

questions.stem: The novel's first sentence is 'They bring her out.' Who is 'her'?
options: A young Iron Age woman about to be sacrificed
Silvie, being brought out of the roundhouse
Molly, being led away by the local police
Silvie's mother, being taken to the hospital
questions.explanation: The prologue opens in the distant past with an unnamed girl. The short, flat sentence makes her a passive victim, and Silvie will later stand in the same place.

questions.stem: Bill tells his family that 'privacy's a fancy modern idea, exactly what we're getting away from'. What does this show?
options: He uses the Iron Age as an excuse to deny his wife and daughter any space of their own
He believes the Iron Age was a time when families had more freedom than today
He is joking about the re-enactment and does not really believe in it at all
He is simply repeating Professor Slade's academic view of family life in Iron Age Britain
questions.explanation: Bill says this early on, at night in the roundhouse. He presents control as authenticity, so 'getting away from' the modern world means getting away from his family's rights.

questions.stem: Bill insists there 'weren't dark faces in these parts for nigh on two millennia'. What does this reveal?
options: His wish to make the re-enactment as historically accurate as it can possibly be
His racist belief in a pure British past, which the novel exposes as a myth
His careful knowledge of the history of Northumberland and its people
His accurate point that ancient Northumberland saw little migration
questions.explanation: Bill wants the past to prove his present prejudices. Hadrian's Wall itself was garrisoned by soldiers from across the Roman Empire, so his claim reveals ideology, not history.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'In Ghost Wall, the past is used as a weapon.' Discuss.
options: Moss shows Bill using an imagined Iron Age to justify his control of his wife and daughter
In Ghost Wall, Silvie and her parents spend two weeks living like people in the Iron Age
This essay will discuss how the past is used as a weapon in Ghost Wall by Sarah Moss
Ghost Wall is a short novel by Sarah Moss that was first published in the year 2018
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Silvie and her mother cook while the men go hunting.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Explain how the division of labour shows Bill using 'tradition' to keep women in their place
Explain that this detail shows how hard and tiring daily life was for people in the Iron Age
Quote the passage where Silvie describes the cooking and the hunting
Describe what the group eats for dinner each night, in order
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the detail suggests. Linking the chores to Bill's control turns an everyday detail into evidence about power.
